title: Inheritance and composition
lesson:
A game has rats, slimes and skeletons. They all have a name and health, they can all be hit, and they all die at 0 hp. Copying that code into three classes means fixing every bug three times. **Inheritance** lets one class build on another:

```
class Enemy:
    def __init__(self, name, hp):
        self.name = name
        self.hp = hp

    def take_hit(self, damage):
        self.hp = max(0, self.hp - damage)

class Slime(Enemy):                 # a Slime IS an Enemy
    def take_hit(self, damage):
        super().take_hit(damage // 2)   # squishy: half damage
```

`Slime(Enemy)` means Slime gets everything Enemy has. Enemy is the **base class** (parent), Slime the **subclass** (child). Writing a method with the same name in the child **overrides** it. `super()` reaches the parent's version, so the child adds its twist without copying the parent's code. A child with its own `__init__` should call `super().__init__(name, hp)` first, so the parent's setup still happens.

The payoff is **polymorphism**: code that works with any Enemy doesn't care which kind it gets.

```
for e in [Enemy("Rat", 5), Slime("Blob", 10)]:
    e.take_hit(4)        # each one reacts in its own way
```

**Composition: has-a instead of is-a.** Inheritance is for "is a kind of": a Slime is an Enemy. Many relationships are "has a": a fighter has a weapon, a robot has two motors, a clinic has a stock list. For those, store one object inside another:

```
class Fighter:
    def __init__(self, name, weapon=None):
        self.name = name
        self.weapon = weapon     # Fighter HAS a Weapon
```

Making `Fighter(Weapon)` would be wrong: a fighter isn't a kind of weapon, and you couldn't swap the spear for a bow during the game. With composition you just do `fighter.weapon = bow`. The professional habit is **prefer composition**, and use inheritance when the "is a" sentence is honestly true and the child really can be used everywhere the parent is.

**Common mistakes**
- Overriding `__init__` and forgetting `super().__init__(...)`: the child object is missing the parent's attributes, and you get AttributeError later.
- Deep chains (A, B(A), C(B), D(C)...). Each layer makes behaviour harder to follow. Two levels is usually plenty.
- Using inheritance only to reuse a helper function. Put the helper in a module or a separate object instead.

**In real programs** game engines use both: a base `Entity` class for things in the world, and components (a health component, a sprite, an AI brain) attached by composition. Robots compose sensors and motors; GUIs subclass a base `Widget`.

notes: Enemy holds what every enemy shares.
Skeleton(Enemy): super().__init__ runs the parent's setup, then adds armor.
Skeleton overrides take_hit but reuses the parent's version through super().
Hero has a Weapon; it is not a Weapon.
One loop, two kinds of enemy: polymorphism.
Composition lets you swap the weapon while the game runs.

exercises.title: Slimes and skeletons
exercises.prompt:
Enemy(name, hp) is given: take_hit(damage) lowers hp (never below 0, negative damage counts as 0) and returns the damage really taken; describe() returns like Rat (5 hp).
Write two subclasses:
- Slime(Enemy): takes half damage, rounded down (damage // 2). Use super().take_hit.
- Skeleton(Enemy) with __init__(self, name, hp, armor=2): call super().__init__, store armor. take_hit takes damage minus armor (never less than 0). describe() returns like Bones (10 hp, armor 2): build it from super().describe().

tests.check:
s = Slime('Blob', 10)
assert isinstance(s, Enemy), 'Slime should inherit from Enemy'
assert s.take_hit(4) == 2 and s.hp == 8, 'a slime hit for 4 takes 2, hp should be 8, got %r' % s.hp
tests.name: slime takes half

tests.check:
k = Skeleton('Bones', 10)
assert isinstance(k, Enemy) and k.name == 'Bones' and k.hp == 10 and k.armor == 2, 'Skeleton needs name, hp (from super().__init__) and armor 2'
k.take_hit(5)
assert k.hp == 7, 'armor 2 blocks 2 of 5 damage, hp should be 7, got %r' % k.hp
tests.name: skeleton armor

tests.check:
assert Enemy('Rat', 5).describe() == 'Rat (5 hp)'
got = Skeleton('Bones', 10).describe()
assert got == 'Bones (10 hp, armor 2)', got
assert Slime('Blob', 3).describe() == 'Blob (3 hp)', 'Slime should keep the parent describe'
tests.name: describe

tests.check:
foes = [Enemy('Rat', 5), Slime('Blob', 10), Skeleton('Bones', 10, armor=3)]
for f in foes:
    f.take_hit(6)
assert [f.hp for f in foes] == [0, 7, 7], [f.hp for f in foes]
tests.name: one loop, three kinds

tests.check:
k = Skeleton('Bones', 10, armor=5)
assert k.take_hit(3) == 0 and k.hp == 10, 'armor bigger than the hit must not heal the skeleton, hp %r' % k.hp
s = Slime('Blob', 4)
s.take_hit(1)
assert s.hp == 4, '1 // 2 is 0 damage'
tests.name: armor never heals

tests.check: assert 'super()' in CODE, 'use super() to reuse the parent methods'
tests.name: uses super()

hints: class Slime(Enemy): def take_hit(self, damage): return super().take_hit(damage // 2)
Skeleton.__init__ starts with super().__init__(name, hp), then self.armor = armor.
For describe, take super().describe(), drop the last ')' with [:-1], and add f", armor {self.armor})".

exercises.title: A fighter has a weapon
exercises.prompt:
Use composition (a Fighter HAS a Weapon; it must not inherit from Weapon).
- Weapon(name, damage, uses): attack() returns damage and uses up one use; with 0 uses left it returns 0. is_broken() is True when uses is 0.
- Fighter(name, weapon=None): stores self.weapon. equip(weapon) sets it.
- strike(target): if the fighter has a weapon that isn't broken, damage = weapon.attack(); otherwise 1 (bare hands). Calls target.take_hit(damage) and returns damage. target is any object with a take_hit method.

tests.check:
w = Weapon('Spear', 6, 2)
assert w.attack() == 6 and w.attack() == 6, 'two uses, 6 damage each'
assert w.attack() == 0 and w.uses == 0 and w.is_broken() is True, 'a used-up weapon does 0 and is broken'
tests.name: weapon uses
bare hands
weapon breaks

tests.check:
assert not issubclass(Fighter, Weapon), 'a Fighter is not a kind of Weapon: store a weapon instead (composition)'
f = Fighter('Amina', Weapon('Bow', 4, 1))
assert isinstance(f.weapon, Weapon) and f.weapon.name == 'Bow'
tests.name: composition

tests.check:
class Dummy:
    def __init__(self):
        self.hits = []
    def take_hit(self, d):
        self.hits.append(d)
d = Dummy()
f = Fighter('Amina', Weapon('Bow', 4, 1))
f.strike(d)
f.equip(Weapon('Club', 9, 5))
f.strike(d)
assert d.hits == [4, 9], d.hits
tests.name: swap weapons

hints: Fighter.__init__ needs self.weapon = weapon; equip just sets self.weapon.
Weapon.attack: if self.uses <= 0 return 0, else take one use and return self.damage.
strike: if self.weapon is not None and not self.weapon.is_broken(): damage = self.weapon.attack(), else damage = 1. Then target.take_hit(damage).

exercises.title: Clinic staff pay
exercises.prompt:
- Staff(name, hourly): class attribute role = "staff". pay(hours) returns hours * hourly. describe() returns like Juma (staff), using self.role.
- Doctor(Staff): role = "doctor". __init__(self, name, hourly, on_call_fee) calls super().__init__. pay(hours) is the normal pay plus on_call_fee.
- Volunteer(Staff): role = "volunteer". __init__(self, name) calls super().__init__ with hourly 0.
- payroll(staff, hours): staff is a list, hours a dict name -> hours worked (missing name means 0). Returns the total pay.

tests.check:
d = Doctor('Wanjiru', 1000, 2000)
assert isinstance(d, Staff), 'Doctor should inherit from Staff'
assert d.pay(8) == 10000, 'pay(8) = 8*1000 + 2000 = 10000, got %r' % d.pay(8)
assert d.describe() == 'Wanjiru (doctor)', d.describe()
tests.name: doctor

tests.check:
v = Volunteer('Juma')
assert isinstance(v, Staff) and v.name == 'Juma' and v.hourly == 0
assert v.pay(10) == 0
assert v.describe() == 'Juma (volunteer)', v.describe()
assert Staff('Amina', 300).describe() == 'Amina (staff)'
tests.name: volunteer and staff

tests.check:
team = [Staff('Amina', 300), Doctor('Wanjiru', 1000, 2000), Volunteer('Juma')]
got = payroll(team, {'Amina': 10, 'Wanjiru': 8, 'Juma': 12})
assert got == 13000, 'expected 3000 + 10000 + 0 = 13000, got %r' % got
tests.name: payroll

tests.check:
team = [Staff('Amina', 300), Doctor('Wanjiru', 1000, 2000)]
got = payroll(team, {})
assert got == 2000, 'nobody worked: only the on-call fee, got %r' % got
assert payroll([], {'Amina': 5}) == 0
tests.name: missing hours
tests.hint_if_fail: hours.get(person.name, 0) gives 0 for someone not in the dict.

tests.check:
assert CODE.count('super().__init__') >= 2, 'Doctor and Volunteer should both call super().__init__'
assert 'role' not in vars(Doctor('a', 1, 1)), 'role should be a class attribute, not set on self'
tests.name: super() and class attributes

hints: A class attribute sits directly under the class line: role = "doctor". self.role finds the child's value first.
Doctor.__init__: super().__init__(name, hourly), then self.on_call_fee = on_call_fee. Doctor.pay: return super().pay(hours) + self.on_call_fee.
payroll: sum(p.pay(hours.get(p.name, 0)) for p in staff)

quiz.q: Which is a good use of inheritance?
quiz.why: A skeleton IS an enemy; the others are has-a relationships.

quiz.q: A child class defines __init__ but never calls super().__init__(). What usually happens?
choices: Attributes the parent sets are missing, so AttributeError later
quiz.why: The parent's setup only runs if you call it.

quiz.q: What does super().take_hit(d) do inside Slime.take_hit?
A loop calls e.take_hit(5) on a mixed list of Enemy, Slime and Skeleton objects. Each reacts its own way. This is called...
quiz.why: Same call, different behaviour per type.

quiz.q: Why prefer composition for a fighter and its weapon?
choices: A fighter isn't a kind of weapon, and you can swap weapons at run time
Inheritance is not allowed in games
quiz.why: Has-a relationships fit composition and stay flexible.

cards.a: Is-a: inheritance (Slime is an Enemy). Has-a: composition (Fighter has a Weapon).
A child class defines a method with the same name, replacing the parent's version.

explain: Explain is-a versus has-a in your own words, with one example of each from a robot or a clinic.
